extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century literate London readers interested in manners, theatre, politics, and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Short topical essays (Tatler-style) addressing theatre, social conduct, politics, and personal conduct, mixing criticism, anecdote, and moral reflection for a general literate public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting: avoid doing too much (no overacting)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is certainly nature excellently represented in his manner of action; in which he ever avoided that general fault in players, of doing too much.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised example: Cave Underhill's natural manner and restraint. Implicit evaluative standard: prefer a natural representation of character over exaggerated gestures or mannerisms; restraint is a mark of good comic acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting: do not add to the author (no ad‑libbing)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It must be confessed, he has not the merit of some ingenious persons now on the stage, of adding to his authors; for the actors were so dull in the last age, that many of them have gone out of the world, without having ever spoke one word of their own in the theatre.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage criticises actors who alter or add lines as a (questionable) 'merit' and admires performers who stick to the author's text; the contextual tone implies fidelity to the script and naturalness are preferred over self‑indulgent interpolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playwriting: avoid stock, telegraphed plots (originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I won't pretend to give you an account of the plot, it being the same design upon which all tragedies have been writ for several years last past; and from the beginning of the first scene, the frequenters of the house may know, as well as the author, when the battle is to be fought, the lady to yield, and the hero to proceed to his wedding and coronation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard for playwrights: avoid recycled, formulaic structures that let audiences predict every major event; strive for novelty or less‑transparent plotting so the drama retains interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting/acting to type: exploit an actor's particular strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Colley Cibber on Underhill: “Underhill was a correct and natural comedian; his particular excellence was in characters that may be called still-life; I mean the stiff, the heavy, and the stupid; to these he gave the exactest and most expressive colours…"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative point: match actors to roles that suit their natural strengths (e.g., still, heavy, or obtuse characters); an actor’s particular physiognomy and style can be a merit when well matched to character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical/persuasive letter standards: moral appeal, measured reproach
rubrics_metrics.description: From the letter to Lewis XIV: the writer admonishes the king to act with sincerity, avoid expecting renown from violence, consider religion and conscience, and not be subject to 'railing accusation'. (“I do not bring against you a railing accusation… as you are a strict professor of religion, I beseech your Majesty to stop the effusion of blood…”)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model for persuasive public correspondence: balance admonition with respect, appeal to shared moral/religious values and long‑term fame, avoid coarse invective; use dignified moral reasoning to persuade rulers or publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character taxonomy: what makes a 'Very Pretty Fellow'
rubrics_metrics.description: “a Very Pretty Fellow… to be allowed as a character by itself, and a person exalted above the other by a peculiar sprightliness, as one who, by a distinguishing vigour, outstrips his companions… admitted at all hours: all he says or does, which would offend in another, are passed over in him; and all actions and speeches which please, doubly please if they come from him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines sociable/personality archetype used in satire and social description: criteria include sprightliness, jaunty behaviour, immunity from offence, favor with women; useful as a rubric for classifying and satirising social figures in essays or caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of a 'Toast' and selection ritual (symbolic criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A toast… elevated into a formal order; and that happy virgin who is received and drank to at their meetings, has no more to do in this life, but to judge and accept of the first good offer. The manner of her inauguration is much like that of the choice of a Doge in Venice: it is performed by balloting… her name is written with a diamond on a drinking-glass. The hieroglyphic of the diamond is to show her, that her value is imaginary; and that of the glass to acquaint her, that her condition is frail…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines cultural ritual and symbolic criteria for being honoured as a 'toast': selection by company ballot, ephemeral reign, and symbolic trappings (diamond, glass) that signal the mock‑valued and fragile nature of the honour—useful when describing social ceremonies or creating satirical portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of duelling: 'satisfaction' as incoherent and dishonourable
rubrics_metrics.description: “As the matter at present stands, it is not to do handsome actions denominates a man of honour; it is enough if he dares to defend ill ones… this resentment neither has its foundation from true reason, nor solid fame; but is an imposture, made up of cowardice, falsehood, and want of understanding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative standard against duelling: the essay furnishes argumentative criteria (reason, true fame, moral standing) to judge duelling as base and irrational. Includes a mock 'challenge' rephrasing to show the absurdity of typical challenge language—a model of rhetorical debunking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice‑giving etiquette: beware solicited counsel after action
rubrics_metrics.description: “some people will ask counsel of you, when they have already acted what they tell you is still under deliberation… I was almost lost a very good friend… I answered, 'By no means…' I saw him moved, and knew from thence he was already determined; therefore evaded it…"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guideline for social conduct and essay anecdotes: recognise when counsel is sought only perfunctorily or post facto; adapt responses (politely evasive or ironic) rather than earnest counsel; useful as a standard for portraying and criticizing social interactions in periodical essays.
